reviews.review: Some of it was fun the first time around, but replaying for achievements made it obvious that this game could have used some reduced railroading.

This game simply did not resonate with me as much as it should have, and I love my privacy. 

I tried out this game because it was on sale on Steam, and I thought this was an interesting game to try out. 

I don't want to write an extensive review because I do not want to give up any more of my time, but this game has (obviously) a limited amount of replay ability. There's only 4 possibly endings, and while I like the ideas that the game was talking about the issues with privacy, I still don't like the game. I typically don't mind reading, but even on the fastest settings it still was to slow to carry on. It felt like the dialogue was dragging even though I understood what the characters in the game were saying.

I didn't really care about the characters. Abraham was cool in a sense where he created this "Thought" activist group and I did want to learn more about what this group does, but I really didn't care for all the other characters.  I just wanted to get the game over with, and it took a confusing amount of time for me to find an ending to the game. 

I'm just glad that i didn't buy the second game.

A terrorist bomb kills a number of people, and it's your job to investigate the suspects - with the help of a handy new government surveillance program that gives you access to their email, their phonecalls, their text messages, their credit card statements, and even data on their personal computers. Add any data that you believe is relevant to their dossiers, while ignoring anything that's not relevant. Another investigator looks at what you've added to their dossiers and gives you tips for what to investigate deeper; he can also draw conclusions from what he sees and call in police action.

The entire game takes place within the Orwell desktop interface. It's beautifully simple and yet gives easy access to all the information you'll need. 'Orwell' is a clever game of finding connections between people, discovering motives, and summarily deciding who's guilty of what ... and, ultimately, passing judgment on whether or not a system like this is a benefit to humanity.

I got every achievement and was away from my desk a few times and still only spent about 10 hours in-game, meaning at full price you're looking at a dollar+ per hour of gameplay. 

There were a couple of frustrating details as well such as unbelievable dialogue in a few places (and do people really have entire websites about their normal run of the mill families?) But it's great for the average sale price.

I did not care for this game so I will place here a recipe for huckleberry pancakes instead.

Huckleberry pancakes.

1 3/4 cups all purpose white flour
4 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1 1/2 cups of buttermilk
5 tablespoon butter, melted
2 large eggs
1/2 cup Huckleberries
In medium bowl combine flour, sugar, baking powder and salt, set aside. In small bowl combine buttermilk, butter and eggs. Add buttermilk mixture to the flour mixture, combine until mixed do not over mix (I prefer to use a whisk it does the best job). Fry at 400 degrees. Pour about 1/4 cup of batter on the griddle and sprinkle with the huckleberries.

Cook on first side about 3 minutes until bubbles appear along the edge of the pancake. Flip and cook for 2 minutes more and golden brown. Serve with a big pat of butter, and some pure maple syrup ( get the real stuff it is worth it).

While the story is interesting and I can see replayability in knowing you've made the wrong move, then creating a new profile and trying to avoid that scenario... I haven't done that. I probably won't either, because I have to agree with other players: the game guides you too much.

You're basically told where to click and when, which completely defeats the point of having all of these fun tools at your disposal--they might as well have dumped all data pieces in a list and had you click on them one by one, all after the other.

The auto-highlighting spoils the point of reading anything. The game warns you that potential choices conflict instead of letting the player decide on how thoroughly they want to investigate before submitting information. Some pieces of info feel completely useless, but your supervisor somehow decides they have more value than they should and the supervisor's decision often feels like a complete whim. And vice-versa: bits of info you feel should be important are locked away or not even meant to be accessible because the game decided "Nope, I won't even let you go into that dead-end for fun".

I guess this was worth what I paid for it... $2! and no more. This had a lot of promise but it doesn't have enough depth or freedom of choice for my tastes.

It took me a bit to get into this game, and some of the interface was confusing at first, but then I really got into it and enjoyed it a lot. The music and sound effects are subtle except when there's a stinger to get your attention, the UI is clean and snappy, the graphics style is pleasing to look at, and the story has a lot of depth and nuance. It's the sort of game that would've been great for my lineup of edutainment games as a teen when I was homeschooling, because of the amount of critical thinking and ethical choice involved. I don't think there's any way to fail a chapter, but I haven't tried inputting all the extraneous info that exists. That said, you WILL need a guide if you want to get all the achievements, and there are some good ones here on Steam. It took me about ten hours to 100%, which isn't bad for what is essentially a visual novel. My only complaint is that I wish the text advancement for things like phone conversations and especially that nearly ten minute call in the last chapter had an option to be even faster. I read quite fast, and especially on replays for achievements I found myself tabbing out and doing other things while letting the conversation roll in the background. That One Call in particular needs a way to skip through it; it was interesting the first time but not the second or third time. It'll take two to three runs of each chapter to get all the achievements.
